column2: Or he may perform only the fivefold placing beginning with the head, and likewise the placing of the six limbs, without the purification of the elements and the rest.
For ascetics it is the placing of dissolution, and likewise for forest-dwellers; for a woman of the household without a husband it is that of maintenance.
Having thus purified body and self in brief form, and attained the state of Shiva, he should worship the supreme Lord.
Now one who has leisure, or whose mind is not confused, should perform the rite of placing by the extended procedure.
There the first is the placing of the letters, next the placing of the Brahmans, third the placing of the pranava, and after that the placing of the hamsa.
The fifth is said by the good to be the placing of the five syllables; of these, one should use one or several in worship and other rites.
Placing a on the head and a on the forehead, i and i on the two eyes, likewise u and u on the two ears,
ri and ri on the cheeks, lri and lri on the two nostrils, e and ai on the two lips, o and au on the two rows of teeth in order,
am on the tongue, then ah on the palate in order; he should place the ka group on the five joints of the right hand,
and the cha group likewise on the joints of the left hand; the ta group and the other ta group on both feet;
pa and pha on the two sides, ba on the back and bha on the navel; he should place ma on the heart, and on the skin and the rest in order
the letters from ya to sa, on the seven bodily elements; ha within the heart, and ksha between the two brows.
For a maiden it is again that of creation. I shall tell the characteristics of the placing: from the thumb to the little finger is declared the placing of maintenance;
Having thus placed the fifty letters by the path of the Rudras, he should place the five Brahmans by the distinction of limb, face and kala.
Having done the placing on the hands and the rest with them, or not, in order, he should assign them to the head, face, heart, private parts and feet.
Then he should assign the faces from the upward one ending with the western; and the five kalas of Ishana on these five in order.
Then on the four faces the four kalas of Purusha should be placed, in the order beginning with the east.
On the heart, throat, shoulders, navel, belly, back and chest — the eight kalas of Aghora — and on the feet and hands too;
then he should contemplate the thirteen kalas of Vamadeva on the anus, the organ, thighs, knees, shanks, buttocks, waist and sides.
The one most versed in ritual should assign the eight kalas of Sadya on the feet, the hands, the nose, the head and the arms. Having thus performed the placing of the thirty-eight kalas in order,
the wise one who knows the pranava should then perform the placing of the pranava: on both arms, the elbows and the wrists,
the sides, belly, thighs and shanks, the feet and the back. Having thus placed the pranava, the one skilled in placing
should perform the placing of the hamsa as described in the Shiva shastra; dividing the seed of the hamsa, on the eyes and nostrils,
beginning from the right thumb and ending with the left thumb is declared the placing of creation; the reverse is dissolution.
dividing it, on the arms, eyes, mouth and forehead, on the ears, armpits, shoulders, sides and breasts,
waist, hands and ankles, or by the path of the five limbs; having done this placing of the hamsa, he should then place the five syllables,

by the path described before, by which Shiva-hood arises. One who is not Shiva should not recite Shiva, one who is not Shiva should not worship Shiva, one who is not Shiva should not meditate on Shiva, and one who is not Shiva cannot attain Shiva.
Therefore, having made the body Shaiva and abandoned the notion of being a bound soul, reflecting "I am Shiva," one should perform the Shaiva rite.
The sacrifice of action, the sacrifice of austerity, next the sacrifice of japa, the sacrifice of meditation and the sacrifice of knowledge — five sacrifices are proclaimed.
Some delight in the sacrifice of action, others in the sacrifice of austerity, others in the sacrifice of japa, and others in the sacrifice of meditation,
and others in the sacrifice of knowledge, each superior to the one before. The sacrifice of action is said to be twofold, with desire and without.
One with desire, having enjoyed his desires, becomes attached to desire again; one without desire, having enjoyed pleasures in Rudra's abode, falls from there
and is born devoted to the sacrifice of austerity, without doubt. The ascetic too, having enjoyed pleasures there and fallen from there,
is born on earth as a man devoted to japa and meditation. A mortal devoted to japa and meditation, by virtue of that excellence here,
He should place the letters beginning with na, with bindu, in order on the fingers, and place Shiva on the palms and on the ring fingers.
gaining knowledge, very soon attains union with Shiva. Therefore even the sacrifice of action, enjoined by Shiva, is liberating for embodied beings;
but one with desire, even though joined to desire, will be only for bondage. Therefore among the five sacrifices one should be devoted to meditation and knowledge.
He who has meditation and knowledge has crossed the ocean of existence. Free of violence and other faults, a pure means for the mind,
the sacrifice of meditation is therefore supreme, granting the fruit of liberation. Just as outside labourers do not greatly share in the fruit,
seen in a king's palace, so here too are those devoted to rites. For meditators the subtle body of the Lord becomes directly visible,
just as here the gross one, fashioned of clay, wood and the like, is for those devoted to rites. Therefore those devoted to the sacrifice of meditation
do not rely greatly on gods of stone and clay, knowing Shiva as he truly is. The man who, abandoning Shiva abiding in the self, worships outside
throws away the fruit in his hand and licks his own elbow. From knowledge comes meditation, and from meditation knowledge arises again;
by both liberation comes; therefore one should be devoted to meditation. At the end of twelve, on the head, the forehead, between the brows,
at the tip of the nose, in the mouth, the neck or the heart, or the navel, the eternal place, with a mind pierced by faith,
Then, having performed the placing of the weapon in the ten directions with the weapon mantra, the five kalas beginning with Nivritti, in the form of the five elements,
he should worship the god and the Goddess with the services of outer worship. Or he should worship daily in a linga or a made image,
in the fire or on an altar, with devotion according to his wealth; or he should worship the supreme Lord both within and without. One devoted to the inner sacrifice may perform outer worship or not.
together with the rulers of the five elements and bearing their respective emblems, resting in the heart, throat, palate, between the brows and at the aperture of Brahman,
he should contemplate their knots with their seeds in those seeds; for their purification he should recite the five-syllabled knowledge.
Restraining the vital breath according to the number of qualities, he should then cut the knot of the elements with the weapon mantra and the weapon gesture.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 7, part 2, chapter 23: the explanation of the rite of worship. Upamanyu said: I shall explain in brief the rite of worship told by Shiva himself to Shiva's consort in the Shiva shastra.
beyond all comparison, with his attendants and his retinue. Then he should contemplate the great Goddess on his left side,
radiant as the petal of a full-blown lotus, with large, long eyes, her face like the full moon, her hair dark and curling,
like the petal of a blue lotus, crowned with the half-moon, her breasts very round, full, high, smooth and ample,
slender-waisted, broad-hipped, in a fine, delicate yellow garment, adorned with every ornament, bright with a tilaka on her forehead,
lovely with her braids strewn with many-coloured flowers, conforming in form in every way, her face bowed a little in modesty,
holding a shining golden lotus in her right hand, her other hand placed like a staff, seated on the great throne,
the very cutter of the noose, whose form is being, consciousness and bliss. Having thus meditated on the god and the Goddess on the excellent auspicious seat,
he should worship them devoutly with flowers of feeling, with all the services. Or, having thus imagined one of the forms of the Lord —
the Shaiva one called Sadashiva, or the supreme Maheshvari, or the one called the twenty-sixth, or the one called Shrikantha —
and having performed the placing of mantras and the rest as on his own body, meditating on Shiva, beyond being and non-being, embodied in this form,
Having performed the inner sacrifice, a subsidiary, ending with the fire rite, or not, he should then perform the outer sacrifice.
he should complete the worship mentally in the order of the outer; then he should contemplate the fire offering in the navel with fuel, ghee and the rest,
and between the brows he should meditate on Shiva in the shape of a pure lamp-flame. Thus in the subsidiary or the independent, in the auspicious yoga of meditation,
ending with the fire rite, the procedure is the same everywhere. Then, having completed the whole mental order of worship,
he should worship the god in a linga, on an altar or in the fire.
There, having mentally imagined and purified the materials, and meditated on and worshipped the god Vinayaka according to rule,
and properly worshipped mentally Nandisha and Suyasha on the south and north, the wise man should imagine a seat,
endowed with worship and the rest — the lion seat, the yoga seat and the like, or a spotless lotus seat possessing the three principles.
Upon it he should meditate on Shiva with Amba, charming in every way, endowed with every auspicious mark, beautiful in every limb,
possessing every excellence, adorned with every ornament, with red mouth, hands and feet, his face smiling like jasmine and the moon,
like pure crystal, with three eyes like full-blown lotuses, four-armed, noble in body, bearing the lovely crescent moon,
his hands showing boon-giving and fearlessness, bearing the deer and the axe, Hara, with serpent necklaces and bracelets, the inside of his throat a lovely blue,
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 7, part 2, chapter 24: the description of the worship of Shiva taught in the shastras. Upamanyu said: He should sprinkle the place of worship with the root mantra for purification, and place a flower there with water of fragrant sandal.
Tips of kusha, unbroken grains, barley, rice and sesame, ghee, white mustard, flowers and ash in the arghya vessel;
kusha, flowers, barley, rice, bahumula and tamala, and ash, he should put into the sprinkling vessel in order.
Placing the mantra in all, encircling them outside with the armour mantra, then protecting them with the weapon mantra, he should show the cow gesture.
Sprinkling all the materials of worship with water from the sprinkling vessel with the root mantra, he should then purify them according to rule.
If the vessels are not available, the excellent practitioner should prepare a single sprinkling vessel for all rites, and the common arghya with water.
Then, having worshipped the god Vinayaka with foods and eatables in order according to rule, beside the door on the right
he should properly worship Nandi himself, ruler of the inner apartments, like a mountain of gold, adorned with every ornament,
crowned with the young moon, gentle, three-eyed and four-armed, the lord bearing a blazing trident, the deer, the axe and a sharp cane,
his face like the orb of the moon, or else like a lion's face; and on the north side of the door, his wife, the daughter of the Maruts,
Suyasha, of good vows, the mother, intent on adorning the feet. Having worshipped her, entering the inner shrine of the Supreme,
Driving away obstacles with the weapon mantra and veiling with the armour mantra, placing the weapon in the directions, he should prepare the ground of worship.
having worshipped the linga with those materials, he should remove the old offerings, and washing a flower, place it on its head for its purification.
With a flower in hand he should recite the mantra according to his ability for the purification of the mantra; worshipping Chanda in the north-east, he should give him the old offerings.
Then he should arrange the seat, beginning with the support, in order; he should meditate on the auspicious dark Adhara Shakti on the ground,
and before her, Ananta with raised neck, coiled, white, five-hooded, as if licking the sky.
Upon him an auspicious seat with four lion feet; dharma, knowledge, dispassion and lordship are its feet,
white, red, yellow and dark in colour, beginning from the south-east; adharma and the rest, from the east to the north in order,
like rajavarta gems, he should place and contemplate as its limbs. Above it as a covering, a spotless white lotus seat;
its eight petals are said to be the eight powers beginning with anima, its filaments the Rudras beginning with Vama, with the Shaktis beginning with Vama;
the seeds too are those same Shaktis, ending with Manonmani; the pericarp is supreme dispassion, the stalk knowledge of Shiva's nature,
the bulb Shiva's dharma, at the end of the pericarp the three orbs; above the three orbs the seat of the three principles beginning with Atma.
Spreading darbha grass there, he should wash with sprinkling and the like; having purified all the vessels, he should purify the materials.
Above all the seats he should arrange a comfortable divine seat, spread with many-coloured coverings, radiant with pure knowledge.
Invocation, installation, confinement, beholding and salutation he should perform, binding the gestures one by one.
Having given water for the feet, sipping water, arghya, fragrance, flowers, then incense, lamp and betel, he should bathe Shiva and his consort.
Or, having arranged the seat and the form thus, and made them whole with the root mantra, the Brahman mantras and others,
he should then invoke with the Goddess Shiva, the supreme cause, like pure crystal, the god unmoving and imperishable,
the cause of all worlds, the supreme one made of all worlds, abiding within and without, pervading, subtler than the atom and greater than the great,
the imperishable Lord, visible to devotees without effort, beyond the reach even of gods such as Brahma, Indra, Vishnu and Rudra,
the essence of the gods, heard by the learned to be beyond reach, without beginning, middle or end, the medicine for those sick with worldly existence,
renowned as the Shiva principle, fixed in the world for the sake of good. With the five services one should devoutly worship the excellent linga,
the linga form of Mahesha, Shiva, the supreme self. At the time of bathing one should make auspicious sounds such as "Victory."
The sprinkling vessel, the arghya vessel, then the foot-water vessel and likewise the vessel for sipping water — these four;
With the five products of the cow, ghee, milk, curd, honey and the like, with roots, the essences of fruits, sesame, mustard and barley meal,
with approved seeds such as barley, and with powders of black gram and the like, having bathed and anointed it with flour and the like, he should bathe it with warm water.
He should rub it with bilva leaves and the like to remove the smell of the unguent, and bathe it again with water, with services fit for an emperor.
He should give fragrant amalaka and turmeric in order; then, cleaning the linga or image with water,
he should bathe it with fragrant water, water with kusha and flowers, and water with gold and gems, consecrated with mantras, in order.
If the materials are not available, he should bathe Shiva with faith with whatever can be gathered, or with water consecrated by mantras alone.
With a pot, a conch, a vardhani vessel, or with the hand, with kusha and flowers, he should bathe it preceded by mantras,
with the Pavamana, the Rudra, the Nila and the Tvarita, with the Linga Sukta and other suktas and with the Atharvashiras,
with the Rik verses and Shaiva Samans, and with the five Brahman mantras, he should bathe the lord of the god of gods, with "Shiva" and the pranava.
As for the god, so he should perform the bathing and the rest for the Goddess; there is no difference there, for the two are alike.
Having washed, sprinkled and looked at them, he should pour auspicious water into them and put in all the holy substances as available:
First performing the bathing and other rites for the god, he should then perform them for the Goddess, by the command of the god of gods.
In worshipping Ardhanarishvara there is no before and after in the services, whether in a linga or anywhere else.
Having performed the ablution of the linga with pure, fragrant water, and wiped it with a cloth, he should give a garment and a sacred thread,
water for the feet, sipping water, arghya, fragrance, flowers and ornaments, incense, lamp, food offering, drinking water, mouth-cleansing,
again sipping water, then mouth-freshener, a splendid, auspicious crown adorned with all jewels,
pure ornaments and garlands of many kinds, fans, chowries, an umbrella, a palm-leaf fan and a mirror;
having given these, he should perform the waving of lights with all auspicious sounds, with song, dance and the like, and cries of victory.
In a vessel of gold, silver or copper, or an auspicious one of clay, adorned with lotuses, flowers, seeds, curd, grains and the like,
marked with a trident, a pair of conches, a lotus, a nandyavarta of cow-dung, the shrivatsa, svastika, mirror, thunderbolt and the fire and other emblems,
placing eight lamps around and one in the middle, he should contemplate and worship in them the nine Shaktis beginning with Vama.
jewels, silver, gold, fragrance, flowers, grains and the like, fruits, sprouts and darbha — holy substances of many kinds.
Covering it with the armour mantra, protecting it on all sides with the weapon mantra and showing the cow gesture, he should lift the vessel with both hands.
Or he may set five lamps on the vessel in order, in the intermediate directions and the middle, or even a single lamp.
Then, lifting that vessel above the linga and the rest in order, he should wave it round three times clockwise with the root knowledge.
Then he should give arghya and fragrant ash on the head; then, having offered a handful of flowers, he should present the offerings.
Then he should give drinking water, and having again given sipping water, he should offer betel with the five fragrant things.
He should sprinkle what is to be sprinkled and have song and dance performed; contemplating Shiva and his consort in the linga and the rest, he should recite Shiva's mantra according to his ability.
Circumambulation, prostration, praise, offering of the self and the making known of one's needs he should perform with humility.
Having given arghya and a handful of flowers and bound the gesture according to rule, he should then ask the god's pardon, dismiss him and contemplate him within himself.
In great difficulty, he may perform the services from water for the feet to mouth-freshener, or from arghya on, or merely the tossing of flowers, with feeling foremost.
By that much alone the supreme dharma is well done in one's feeling. One should not eat without worshipping Shiva, as long as breath moves.
In the bathing water, fragrance and the like, and especially in the drinking water, he should put cool, lovely flowers and the like.
If a sinner eats wilfully, there is no expiation for him; if he eats through negligence, he should vomit it up with effort,
bathe, worship the god and the Goddess twice as much, fast, and recite Shiva's mantra ten thousand times, preceded by celibacy.
The next day, giving gold and the like according to his ability to Shiva or to a devotee of Shiva, and performing a great worship, he becomes pure.
In the foot-water he should put vetiver and sandal; jati, kankola, camphor, bahumula and tamala,
ground fine, he should put especially into the sipping water; cardamom, camphor and sandal into all the vessels.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 7, part 2, chapter 25: the description of worship as taught in the Shiva shastras. Upamanyu said: What has not been said here about worship, as if from fear of breaking the order, I shall now tell in brief and not at length.
with folded hands, seated at ease, are to be meditated upon. With the names of all the deities of the enclosures joined to "namah,"
he should worship them with flowers, bowing to all in order. He may worship only the innermost enclosure, or with his own enclosure.
In yoga, meditation, japa and fire offering, outer or inner, the oblation to be given is of six kinds: pure rice, rice with green gram,
sweet rice, rice mixed with curd, rice with jaggery, and rice steeped in honey; one or several of these, with various relishes,
with jaggery and sugar, he should give, and excellent churned curd; foods chief among them cakes, and tasty fruits,
very cool drinking water rich with red sandal and flowers, soft pieces of areca nut soaked in cardamom juice,
betel leaves with catechu and the like, white and golden, auspicious and prescribed, and white lime from stone, neither too dry nor spoiled;
camphor, kankola, jati and the like, fresh and auspicious; the unguent should be sandal, the root wood powdered;
musk, saffron, the essence of musk; flowers fragrant, pure and auspicious.
Flowers that are scentless or harsh-smelling, spoiled, stale or fallen apart of themselves should not be offered in Shiva's worship.
Before the offering of oblation and after the offering of lamps, or when the waving of lights has come, he should perform the worship of the enclosures.
Garments should be soft and made of gold thread, and ornaments especially like rings of lightning.
All these should be fumigated with camphor, resin, aloe and sandal, and scented all around with masses of flowers.
Incense made of powders of sandal, aloe, camphor wood and guggulu, with ghee and honey, is praised.
Lamps always lit with very fragrant ghee from a tawny cow, with camphor, are commended.
The five products of the cow, sweet milk, curd and ghee from a tawny cow are dear to Shambhu for bathing and drinking.
Auspicious seats of ivory, set with gold and jewels, and many-coloured coverings,
with soft pillows, of fine cotton, lofty and low, lovely and comfortable beds;
water brought from a river flowing to the sea or a stream, cool and strained through cloth, is excellent for bathing and drinking.
An umbrella like the moon, lovely, shining with strings of pearls, set with the nine gems, divine, charming with a golden handle;
chowries white and fine, decorated with gold, in the shape of a pair of royal swans, adorned with jewelled handles;
There, in the first enclosure of Shiva or of Shiva's consort, he should worship from Ishana to Sadya, and from Rudra to the weapon.
a mirror, very smooth, anointed with divine fragrance, set with jewels all around and adorned with fine garlands;
a conch of deep sound, like a swan, jasmine or the moon, inlaid with jewels and gold at the mouth, back and other parts;
lovely trumpets producing many sounds, made of gold and adorned with pearls;
kettledrums, mridangas, murajas, timichchhas, patahas and the like, with a sound like the ocean, should be carefully provided.
Lovely utensils and vessels in their entirety, and all their stands, should be made of gold.
The temple of Mahesha, Shiva, the supreme self, should be built like a royal palace, with the characteristics described in the shastra of crafts,
surrounded by high walls, with gateways like mountains, covered with many jewels, with golden doors and panels,
made of refined gold, surrounded by hundreds of jewelled pillars, rich in canopies of pearl strings, with doorways and arches of coral,
its top adorned with divine golden crowns shaped like pots, marked with the king of weapons,
adorned on all sides with dwellings fit for princes and royal streets, and with lofty mansions with tall peaks,
In the north-east, in the east, the south and the north, the west, the south-east, the north-east and the south-west,
with excellent halls of audience standing in the directions and intermediate directions, its outskirts highly adorned as if with inner enclosures,
with thousands of excellent women skilled in dance and song, and many men skilled in flute and vina,
guarded by heroic guards with elephants, horses and chariots, with many flower gardens and many lakes,
shining in the directions and intermediate directions with many long ponds; served by brahmins who know the truth of the Vedas and Vedanta, devoted to the Shiva shastras,
devotees delighting in Shiva's order, with the marks described in the Shiva shastra, peaceful, smiling, prosperous and devoted to good conduct,
glorious Shaivas and Maheshvaras. Thus, within and without, with whatever has been built according to one's ability,
in a place of stone, ivory, wood or brick, or simply of clay, or in a holy forest or on a mountain,
by a river, in a temple, elsewhere, or in an auspicious house — whether rich or poor, not stinting one's own ability, one should worship the god devoutly with materials lawfully acquired.
Even if one worships Shiva devoutly with unlawfully acquired things, there is no fault for him, since the Lord is won by feeling.
If one worships without devotion even with lawfully acquired things, one does not obtain its fruit; devotion alone is the cause here.
in the north-west and again the north-east, and after that in the four directions — this is called the innermost enclosure, or the collection of mantras.
Whatever is done with devotion for Shiva according to one's wealth, small or great, bears equal fruit for rich and poor.
A man of little wealth should do it, urged by devotion; even one of great wealth should not do it without devotion.
Whoever gives even his all to Shiva without devotion does not share its fruit; devotion alone is the cause here.
Not by the fiercest austerities nor by all the great sacrifices can one go to Shiva's divine city without devotion to Shiva.
More secret than the secret, O Krishna, everywhere, is devotion to Shiva, the supreme Lord; there is no doubt: joined with it one is liberated.
The japa of Shiva's mantra, meditation, fire offering, sacrifice, austerity, learning, giving and study — all are for the sake of feeling; there is no doubt.
A man without feeling is not liberated even if he does everything; one with feeling is liberated even without doing anything.
What need has a devotee of Shiva of thousands of chandrayanas, hundreds of prajapatyas, month-long fasts and the rest?
Men without devotion perform austerities in this world and in mountain caves for petty enjoyments; the devotee is liberated through feeling.
Sattvic action gives liberation, and yogis abide in sattva; those devoted to rites, veiled by rajas, perform rajasic action that gives powers.
Or he may worship from the heart to the weapon. Outside that, he should worship Shakra in the east and Yama in the south,
Asuras and rakshasas, endowed with tamas, worship the Lord for worldly ends, and other men of that kind too.
Whether resorting to a tamasic, rajasic or sattvic disposition, one who performs worship and the rest with devotion attains good.
Since devotion is made like a boat to carry one across the ocean of sin, what harm can rajas and tamas do to one endowed with devotion?
Whether outcaste, lowly, fool or fallen, if one has taken refuge in Shiva, O Krishna, he is worthy of honour by all gods and asuras.
Therefore one should worship Shiva with devotion alone, with every effort, since for those without devotion there is no fruit anywhere.
I shall tell you a very great secret — hear my words, Krishna — well settled after consideration by the Vedas, the shastras and those who know the Veda.
the wise man should worship Varuna in the west and Kubera in the north, Isha in the north-east, Agni in his own quarter, and Nirriti in the south-west,
Maruta in the north-west, Vishnu in the south-west and Brahma in the north-east; outside the lotus, the weapons from the thunderbolt to the lotus,
of well-known forms, he should worship in the directions of the world-guardians in order. All the deities of the enclosures, looking toward the god and the Goddess,
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 7, part 2, chapter 26: the description of the rite of worship with its limbs and subsidiary limbs. Upamanyu said: Whether a slayer of a brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief, one who violates his guru's bed, a matricide, a patricide, a slayer of heroes or of an embryo,
He should worship the god with the six syllables or the sukta mantra — a devotee of Shiva who has conquered anger, whether he has received it or not.
One who has received it is superior to one who has not, without doubt; with it, together with the Brahma-limbs and the hamsa, one is liberated.
Therefore one should always worship Shiva with devotion with the sukta mantra, once a day, twice, three times or constantly.
Those who worship Mahadeva are to be known as Maheshvaras. By one who has not worshipped the blessed Shiva with knowledge as his companion,
he wanders long in this worldly existence, an ocean of sorrow. The fool who, having obtained rare human birth, does not worship Shiva —
his birth is fruitless, since it does not lead to liberation. Those who, having obtained rare human birth, worship the Pinaka-bearer —
their birth is fruitful; those best of men have fulfilled their purpose. Those devoted to Bhava, whose minds bow to Bhava,
intent on remembering Bhava, do not partake of sorrow. Charming mansions, women with dazzling ornaments,
and wealth to the point of satiety are the fruit of the rite of Shiva's worship. Those who desire great pleasures and kingship in the abode of the gods
long always for the lotus feet of Hara. Good fortune, radiant beauty, strength, a generous heart,
having worshipped Shiva, the supreme cause, with devotion even without mantra, is freed from those sins gradually in twelve years.
valour and fame in the world come to one who worships Shiva. Therefore, abandoning everything, with mind fixed on Shiva alone,
one should perform the rite of Shiva's worship if one desires good for oneself. Life passes swiftly, youth passes swiftly,
sickness comes swiftly; therefore the Pinaka-bearer is to be worshipped. As long as death has not come, as long as old age has not overtaken you,
as long as the senses have not failed, worship Shankara. There is no other dharma in the three worlds equal to the worship of Shiva.
Knowing this, Sadashiva is to be worshipped with effort. The worship at the door, the curtain, the bali offering to the retinue
and the daily festival should be performed if one worships in a temple. After the offering of oblation, oneself or an attendant
should offer bali in order to the retinue of the temple; going out with music and standing facing that direction,
he should give flower, incense, lamp and food with water; then, standing at the great pedestal facing north, he should give bali.
Then whatever food and the like was offered to the god before — all of it, or what remains — he should offer to Chanda.
Having made offerings according to rule, he should then complete the rest of the worship. Having performed the application according to rule and recited the mantra,
Therefore even a fallen man should worship Shiva with every effort — if he is a devotee, and no other — living on alms, with senses conquered.
he should perform the daily festival as described in Shiva's teaching. In a large metal vessel adorned with red lotuses
he should invoke and worship the divine Pashupata weapon, and place that vessel on the head of an adorned brahmin,
his body placed with the weapon, bearing a blazing staff; outside the temple retinue, with auspicious sounds,

Having performed circumambulation and the rest as described before in order, taking eight flowers, he should then conclude the worship.
Even having committed a very great sin, if one worships the lord of gods with devotion with the five syllables, one is freed from that sin.
Those who live on water or air and others emaciated by vows do not reach Shiva's world by these vows.
But whoever worships Shiva even once with devotion with the five syllables alone goes to Shiva's abode through the greatness of Shiva's mantra.
Therefore austerities and all sacrifices with the gift of all one's wealth as fee are not equal to a ten-millionth part of the worship of Shiva's image.
Whether bound or freed from the noose, if a devotee worships with the five syllables he is liberated; there is no need to deliberate on this.
Whether without Rudra's initiation or with it, whoever worships Shiva even once with the sukta, even if fallen or foolish, is liberated.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 7, part 2, chapter 27: the description of the fire rite. Upamanyu said: Now I shall tell of the fire rite, in a fire-pit or on an altar, on a raised platform, or in a new auspicious vessel of iron or clay.
A mandala with cow-dung and water — the measure of the vessel is not stated. He should plaster a clay fire-pit or altar with cow-dung and water.
Washing the vessel, he should heat it and sprinkle it with other water; then he should draw the lines in the fire-pit and the rest in the manner stated in his own sutra.
Sprinkling it, he should arrange a seat for the fire with darbha or flowers; he should prepare all the materials for worship and for the fire offering.
Washing what is to be washed and sprinkling with the sprinkling water, he should purify them. Fire produced from a gem or from wood, or taken from a Vedic scholar's house,
or another honoured fire, he should then bring with its holder; going round three times clockwise above the fire-pit and the rest in order,
uttering the fire seed, he should set the fire on its seat, by the path of the yoni, or likewise facing himself.
The wise man should make the whole fire-pit located at the yoni region. He should remember the fire within his own navel, coming out through its opening like a spark,
merged into the outer fire, in the shape of an orb. Up to the consecration of the ghee, preceded by the laying of fuel,
the mantra-knower should proceed in the order stated in his own sutra with the root mantra. Having worshipped Shiva's form, then on the right side
placing the mantra in the ghee, he should show the gesture called the cow. The ladle and spoon should be of metal, not of bronze, iron or lead,
Having established the fire according to rule and consecrated it, and worshipped Mahadeva there, he should perform the fire offering.
or made of sacrificial wood, as in the smritis, or approved by craftsmen; or a leaf of the brahma tree and others, without holes, raised in the middle.
Wiping them with darbha, heating them in the fire, he should sprinkle them again; sprinkling around in the order stated in his own sutra, preceded by Shiva's name,
he should make offerings with the eight seeds for the consecration of the fire: bhrum, stum, brum, shrum in order, then pum, drum, drum,
the seven seeds of the seven tongues in succession. The three-crested middle tongue is called Bahurupa;
its crest blazing on the right and another on the left; Hiranya is the north-eastern tongue, Kanaka stands in the east,
Rakta in the south-east, Krishna in the south-west, and another is held to be Suprabha; the extra one, the tongue of the wind, has a radiance according to its name.
They should be spoken after their own seeds, ending with "svaha," in order; having offered ghee with the tongue mantras, to each tongue one by one in order,
and having offered three oblations in the middle with "ram vahnaye svaha," he should sprinkle around with ghee or with fuel-sticks.

When this is done, it becomes the Shiva fire; he should remember Shiva's seat there, invoke there and worship the god Shiva as Ardhanarishvara. Having sprinkled around up to the lamp, he should then perform the offering of fuel-sticks.
They should be of palasha or another sacrificial wood, twelve fingers long, not crooked, not dried of themselves, with bark, unblemished and even,
The fire-pit should be two cubits or one cubit in size, round or square; he should make an altar and a mandala.
or ten fingers long as prescribed, the thickness of the little finger, or a span long if these are not available; all should be offered.
He should then give the ghee oblation, shaped like a durva leaf and four fingers long, and then food the size of a die,
likewise parched grain, mustard, barley and sesame, and foods smeared with ghee, things to be licked and sucked if available.
Ten oblations should be offered there, or five or three, according to one's ability; or one may give only a single oblation.
Ghee with the spoon, fuel-sticks and the like with the ladle, the rest with the hand; the offering there should be made with the divine or the sages' part of the hand.
Or, if others are not available, he should offer again with faith with a single substance; for atonement he should consecrate and offer three oblations.
Then, filling the ladle with the ghee left from the offering, placing a flower at its tip, with the spoon face down upon it,
covering it with darbha, rising with cupped hands with the root mantra ending in "vaushat," he should pour a stream the size of a barley grain.
Having thus made the full oblation, he should sprinkle around as before; then, dismissing the lord of gods, he should preserve the fire.
Or, dismissing it too, he should worship it daily, joining it in the navel. Or, bringing the fire by the path described in the Shiva shastra,
The fire-pit should be wide and deep, with an eight-petalled lotus in its middle, four fingers high or two fingers.
